newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Russian premier says no swerving from reform.
newsitem.headline: Russian premier says no swerving from reform.

text.p: Russia's Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin said on Thursday President Boris Yeltsin was exercising his powers at the helm of state and pledged there would be no deviation from reform.

Chernomyrdin also told a news conference at the Davos World Economic Forum that he expected foreign investment in Russia would surge from $2 billion in 1994 and $6 billion last year to $20 billion by the end of the century.
Asked if the ailing Kremlin chief was able to handle state affairs while his prime minister was out of the country, Chernomyrdin replied: "Yes, he can and he is doing it."
He added: "If there had been any doubt, and if there had been any problem, I would not have come to Davos."

Chernomyrdin, attending the gathering of political and business leaders for the third time, said on return to Moscow on Saturday, Yeltsin's birthday, he would go to congratulate the President "with a bouquet of flowers and a gift."
"Let us all wish him a speedy recovery....Anyone takes time to get over pneumonia," he added.

He said Yeltsin, who went to the Kremlin earlier on Thursday for talks apparently intended to show he was firmly in charge, would meet President Jacques Chirac of France at the weekend and U.S. President Bill Clinton in Moscow as scheduled in March.
Chirac will be the first Western leader to see the 66-year-old Yeltsin since he fell ill last month, soon after returning to work from a heart bypass operation.
But, answering questions, Chernomyrdin implicitly rejected any suggestion that there could be domestic policy changes in Russia if the president were for any reason to leave his post.
"A president in any country is the guarantee of political and social stability," he told the news conference after addressing the opening session of the week-long Forum.
But the country would never return to its communist past. "There can be no going back for us under any circumstances," he declared.
"Russia will not swerve from the path of democratic reform and of creating a strong market economy."

Chernomyrdin said the government's efforts to build up a powerful economy with a firm legal base and open to the outside world would increasingly attract foreign investors, who put in only $2 billion in 1995 and $6 billion last year.
"We are setting up the structures they want to see," he said. "This will give them more confidence....
"I am sure, I am certain, that by the year 2000 it (foreign investment) will reach $20 billion," he added. "There are still problems but we will overcome them."

The Russian prime minister reiterated Moscow's strong disapproval of the extension of the West's NATO alliance to his country's borders through admission to membership to former Soviet bloc states in Europe.
He said NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, who speaking from the same Forum platform earlier had argued the alliance's expansion plans would increase European security, "is wrong."

With the end of the Cold War following the collapse of the old communist system, he said, Europe had no dividing lines but one would be created again if NATO "which has not yet changed its nature" came to Russia's frontier.

"Russia does not want a new dividing line," Chernomyrdin declared, telling a Bulgarian journalist that her country and others like Poland seeking NATO membership would not gain from going in but might lose.
Russia, he added, was ready to join the NATO Council as a full member, taking the body from 16 to 17 members. But it would not accept NATO's current "16 plus one" formula.
